pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** Relative Motion

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, KS3 Physics — Motion):** Relative motion — trains and cars passing one another; describing an object's motion relative to a chosen reference point and recognising that the description depends on the observer's frame.

- **Standards — US (NGSS — Frames of Reference, extends HS-PS2 Motion and Stability):** Describing the motion of an object relative to a chosen reference frame; recognising there is no single privileged frame (foundational kinematics introduced at MS when describing motion, formalised at HS).

- **Operational details:** Relative motion is the idea that the apparent speed and direction of an object depend on the observer's own motion — there is no single 'true' motion, only motion measured relative to a chosen frame of reference. The central instructional habit to build is asking 'moving relative to what?' for every description of motion. The most powerful teaching tool is letting pupils SWITCH the observer's frame on the same scene (stand on the platform vs ride the train) and see how the description changes, supported by careful teacher language: words like 'see', 'appears', 'stationary' or 'standing still' used without naming a frame quietly reinforce the misconception that there is a privileged, absolute (usually Earth) frame. Quantitatively, relative speed is found by subtracting velocities when objects move the same way and adding them when they move towards/away from each other.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). Relative motion is a threshold concept requiring the learner to decentre from their own frame: the milestone is internalising 'moving relative to what?' and accepting that there is no privileged, absolute (Earth) frame. At 11–12 this is early-formal — pupils can switch the observer on the same scene and see descriptions change, and begin the add/subtract relative-speed rule, but the intrinsic-motion intuition (and granting Earth a special status) persists well beyond this age and must be actively confronted.
bestPractices: Make 'relative to what?' a constant refrain; always name the frame, even when it is the Earth, to counter the belief that motion is absolute.
Let pupils switch frames on the SAME scenario (platform observer vs train passenger) rather than viewing a single fixed outcome — the comparison is where the concept lives.

Use the OpenStax embodied demo: a pupil stands as 'the background' while the teacher walks between them and the class; the class says 'to the right', the background pupil says 'to the left' — then state explicitly that the reference frame is the observer's viewpoint, not the background.
Use canonical everyday scenarios: two trains alongside each other, a passing car, a boat crossing a river; have pupils predict-observe-explain each observer's account.
Mind language: avoid bare 'it is moving / it is stationary'; model 'moving relative to the platform but stationary relative to the other train'.
For relative speed, build the add/subtract rule from concrete cases (two trains side by side at the same speed appear still to each other → subtract; trains approaching → add).
keyRepresentations: Side-by-side two-frame view: the same scene rendered from each observer's viewpoint
Train-alongside-train and platform scenario (the canonical relative-motion vehicle)
Labelled velocity arrows with explicit subscripts (e.g. 'train relative to platform', 'boat relative to water')
Number line for adding/subtracting velocities to get relative speed
commonMisconceptions: Motion is intrinsic to an object — treating velocity/trajectory as a property the object 'has', not a quantity measured relative to a frame (Saltiel & Malgrange; ages 11 to university).
Distinguishing 'real' motion (dynamically caused) from 'apparent' motion ('just an optical illusion'), instead of all motion being frame-relative.
Granting the Earth a privileged or absolute frame of reference.
Treating the reference frame as the BACKGROUND/scenery of motion rather than the observer's viewpoint (OpenStax).
Treating a frame as fixed to and bounded by a concrete object ('a ball thrown can leave the reference frame'), with limited physical extent.
Assuming each observer is a separate frame even when observers are at rest relative to one another (they share a frame).

learn.summary: Relative motion for 11–12 year olds: the apparent speed and direction of an object depend on the observer's chosen frame of reference, so there is no single 'true' motion. The core instructional habit is to ask 'moving relative to what?' for every description, and the pivotal experience is switching the observer on the SAME scene (platform vs train passenger) so the description changes while nothing physical about the objects changes. Learners also build the quantitative rule: subtract the speeds for objects moving the same way, and add them for objects moving towards or away from each other in opposite directions; the same-speed same-direction case gives zero relative speed (one appears stationary). Guidance confronts persistent intuitions that motion is intrinsic, that the Earth is a privileged frame, that the reference frame is the background scenery rather than the observer's viewpoint, and that one view is the 'real' motion while another is a mere optical illusion.

activities.title: Switch the observer on the same train scene
feedback: If a learner says one train is 'really' moving, ask 'moving relative to what?' and have them re-describe it from the other train's viewpoint so each train becomes 'the mover' in turn.
When a learner reads motion off the scenery, point out the chosen frame is the observer's viewpoint, not the trees or ground; show that with two trains and no visible ground the view is symmetric.
For the same-speed, same-direction case, highlight that the relative speed reads zero, which is why Train B hangs still beside Train A's window.
For the oncoming case, draw attention to the larger relative speed and connect it to adding the speeds.
activities.rationale: The concept is that the same motion is described differently from a different frame, so letting learners change the observer and watch the apparent velocities recompute targets the 'motion is intrinsic' and 'Earth is the true frame' intuitions directly, and the scenery-vs-viewpoint feedback addresses the background misconception. Carrying the same reasoning to the passing car and boat-crossing-river cases shows the idea generalises. The frame toggle, apparent-velocity labels, subscripts and relative-speed readout are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory features.
sourceClaims: Students treat motion as intrinsic rather than frame-relative; grant the Earth a privileged frame; treat frames as fixed to and bounded by concrete objects; many cannot apply a reference frame even after instruction.

Students assume a reference frame is the background of motion instead of the observer's viewpoint; the walk-across-the-room demo (background pupil sees 'left', class sees 'right') corrects this, concluding the frame is the viewpoint of the observer.
learnerActions: Watch a scene of two trains on parallel tracks beside a platform, with all objects at rest before the motion begins.

Choose a viewpoint — RIDE TRAIN A, RIDE TRAIN B, or STAND ON PLATFORM — and observe how the SAME physical motion is re-described from that viewpoint: e.g. riding Train A, the platform and scenery slide backwards and Train B (moving at the same speed and direction) appears frozen alongside; on the platform, both trains move.
For each viewpoint, read the apparent-velocity labels and relative-speed readout, which use explicit subscripts (e.g. 'Train B relative to Train A', 'train relative to platform').
Switch to an 'approaching/oncoming' setup and compare: two trains going the same way show a small relative speed; two oncoming trains show a large one.

Try the same frame-switch reasoning on other everyday scenarios — a car passing you on the road, or a boat crossing a river (its motion looks different relative to the water than relative to the bank) — to see the idea is not special to trains.
Before each switch, predict out loud what the chosen observer will see, then check against the scene.
State, in words, the frame for every description (e.g. 'Train B is stationary relative to Train A but moving relative to the platform').
activities.intendedInsight: The same motion looks different from different frames; nothing about the trains changes when you switch observers — only who is watching. Motion is always 'relative to' a chosen frame, not an intrinsic property, and the Earth/ground is just one frame among many.

activities.title: Walk-across-the-room: viewpoint vs background
feedback: If pupils equate the frame with the background, contrast the seated class (walker moving) with the pupil walking alongside (walker staying beside them): the background did not change, only the observer's motion did. If pupils cite the class and the background pupil saying 'right' versus 'left', point out that this is a difference in facing direction, not in frame.

For the side-by-side walkers, note that 'the other one looks stationary' (relative speed zero) surfaces the frame idea, whereas 'the same speed as we see them' reflects an absolute-motion assumption to be examined.
activities.rationale: This embodied demonstration gives learners a direct, physical experience of two observers in different states of motion describing one walk differently but equally validly, confronting the misconception that the frame is the background scenery and separating a genuine frame difference from a mere left/right facing difference. The predict-observe-explain structure makes each observer's account explicit.
sourceClaims: Students assume a reference frame is the background of motion instead of the observer's viewpoint; the walk-across-the-room demo (background pupil sees 'left', class sees 'right') corrects this, concluding the frame is the viewpoint of the observer.
learnerActions: One pupil stands still to act as 'the background'; the teacher (or another pupil) walks steadily between that pupil and the class, while a second pupil walks alongside the walker at the same pace as a moving observer.

The seated class describes the walker as moving across the room; the moving observer describes the walker as staying beside them. The background pupil may say 'to the left' where the class says 'to the right' only because they face the other way: they are at rest relative to the class, so they share the class's frame and agree the walker is moving at the same speed.
Compare the two descriptions of the exact same walk and discuss why they differ.
State explicitly that the reference frame is set by the observer's own motion, not by the background pupil, the scenery, or which way the observer is facing.
Extend: walk two pupils side by side at the same steady pace and have the class predict how fast each walker sees the OTHER moving, and why, before asking the walkers.
activities.intendedInsight: A reference frame is set by the observer's own motion, not by the background or scenery. Observers moving differently (the seated class and the pupil walking alongside) give different but equally valid descriptions of the same walk; observers at rest relative to each other share a frame, even if facing opposite ways makes their left/right words differ.

activities.title: Compute relative speed: add or subtract?
feedback: If a learner always adds the two speeds, test their rule on the same-speed same-direction case: adding would give double the speed, but the correct relative speed is zero because they appear stationary to each other — so same direction must subtract.
For the oncoming pair at 50 and 40, confirm the closing speed is 50 + 40 = 90; for the same-direction pair, the difference is 50 − 40 = 10.
Always ask which object the relative speed is measured relative to, so the number is tied to a frame.
activities.rationale: The add/subtract rule is best built from concrete cases rather than stated as a formula, and the same-speed same-direction 'appears stationary' result both anchors subtraction and connects back to the frame-toggle scene. A number line makes the add-vs-subtract contrast visual. Explicitly testing the faulty 'always add' habit against the zero-relative-speed case targets a documented error pattern.
learnerActions: Work through the same-direction case: two trains (or cars) travelling the same way at the same speed — compute the relative speed and confirm it is zero, so each appears stationary to the other.
Work through two cars driving side by side at the same 60 mph: state how fast each appears to move as seen from the other, and explain why it looks stationary.

Work through an oncoming case: two cars approach each other, one at 50 and one at 40 — compute how fast they close on each other (50 + 40 = 90), then redo it for both going the same way (50 − 40 = 10, closing if the faster is behind or separating if it is ahead).

Optionally use a number line: mark where each car is after one hour from where they started. In opposite directions the distance between them changes by both distances together (50 + 40 = 90), while in the same direction it changes only by the difference (50 − 40 = 10).
State the rule in your own words: same direction → subtract the speeds; towards or away in opposite directions → add the speeds.
Name the frame for each answer (e.g. 'relative to the other car').
activities.intendedInsight: Relative speed is found by subtracting the speeds when objects move the same way and adding them when they move towards or away from each other in opposite directions; the same-speed same-direction case gives zero relative speed (appears stationary).

activities.title: The ambiguous two-train departure
feedback: If a learner insists one train is 'really' moving regardless of frame, have them re-tell the scene from each frame so each train becomes 'the mover', and require the frame to be named every time.
If a learner reads the motion off the background scenery, strip the scenery away (two trains, no visible ground) to show the motion is symmetric.

If a learner tries to resolve the ambiguity by calling one view 'real' and the other 'just an optical illusion', clarify that neither description is a mere illusion: both are equally valid relative to their frames, so the fix is to name the frame, not to decide which view is the real motion.

Use the steady-straight-line train question to surface that, for steady straight-line motion and without an outside reference, no internal observation singles out one frame as 'truly' moving; changes in speed or direction can be felt, which is a separate idea.
activities.rationale: This diagnostic scenario discriminates between learners who treat motion as absolute (and privilege the ground/Earth or the scenery) and those who accept frame-relativity and resolve ambiguity by naming a frame. Working from both frames enforces the 'relative to what?' habit, and the optical-illusion feedback confronts the related 'real vs apparent motion' misconception (a pedagogy-level misconception, not drawn from a cited source).
sourceClaims: Students treat motion as intrinsic rather than frame-relative; grant the Earth a privileged frame; treat frames as fixed to and bounded by concrete objects; many cannot apply a reference frame even after instruction.
learnerActions: Consider: two trains sit side by side at a platform; yours begins to move smoothly, and looking only out of the window at the other train, it seems as though the OTHER train is sliding backwards.
Explain how the same view can mean either 'we are moving' or 'they are moving', and what decides which is true.
Resolve the ambiguity by naming a frame: relative to the platform/ground, whichever train's position changes is the mover; relative to the other train, each sees the other move.
Answer a paired question from two frames: 'You're on the train — is the platform moving?' answered from the train's frame AND from the platform's frame.

Discuss: is there any experiment inside a train moving at a steady speed in a straight line that could tell you you're moving, without looking outside? (Speeding up, braking or going round a bend can be felt, so keep the question to steady straight-line motion.)
activities.intendedInsight: Looking only at the other train, your train going forwards and their train going backwards look identical — the view is genuinely ambiguous. There is no single 'really moving' answer without saying relative to what.

activities.title: Check and consolidate frame reasoning
feedback: For 'same speed, same direction', the expected answer is that Train B appears stationary (relative speed zero); if a learner adds the speeds, revisit the subtract rule.
For the 'name the frame' prompts, treat any description without a named frame as incomplete, even when the frame is the Earth.
If a learner says two observers at rest relative to each other are separate frames, point out they share a frame because neither moves relative to the other.
activities.rationale: Frame reasoning and relative-speed arithmetic are readily assessable, so a focused check after the interactive work confirms transfer. It tests and consolidates the perspective shift rather than building it, so it should follow the switchable scene and embodied demo rather than replace them.
sourceClaims: After instruction over 2/3 of physics undergraduates and 1/3 of graduate students could not apply a reference frame to judge simultaneity; observers at rest relative to one another share a frame.
learnerActions: Answer: 'A passenger on Train A looks at Train B moving at the same speed and direction — what do they see?' and justify in terms of relative speed.
Use a slider or fill-in to give the relative speed for an approaching pair versus a same-direction pair, explaining the choice of add or subtract.
Match each observer (e.g. platform observer, Train A passenger, Train B passenger) to their correct description of a given motion.
Complete 'name the frame' prompts for several everyday descriptions, filling the blank in 'moving relative to ___'.
Decide whether two observers who are at rest relative to one another count as one frame or two, and explain.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can apply the 'relative to what?' habit and the add/subtract rule across new cases, and recognise that observers at rest relative to one another share a frame.

constraints: Always name the frame in descriptions of motion — even when it is the Earth — and avoid bare 'it is moving' or 'it is stationary'; teacher language using 'see', 'appears', 'stationary' without a named frame quietly reinforces the belief in a privileged absolute (Earth) frame.

The learning lives in the COMPARISON of frames on the same scenario (platform vs passenger); a single fixed outcome does not let learners see the description change, so provide a way to re-describe the same motion from more than one viewpoint.

A static two-panel 'from the platform / from the train' picture with tap-to-reveal can illustrate the contrast as a recap reference, but it does not let learners re-run the scene from a new viewpoint, so it works as a scaffold rather than the main route to the perspective shift.

A recognition-only quiz tests frame reasoning and relative-speed arithmetic but does not by itself elicit the learner's independent construction of a frame-switch; use it as a check after hands-on or interactive work.

Relative motion is a threshold concept at this age: intrinsic-motion intuition and granting Earth special status persist beyond 11–12 and must be actively and repeatedly confronted, not assumed fixed after one lesson.

Distinguish the chosen frame from the scenery/background — a frame is set by the observer's own state of motion (for example, riding with Train A or standing on the platform), not by what lies in the background, where the observer stands, or which way they face; a frame can be attached to an object such as a train, but it is not limited to that object's physical size.

For young learners, be precise about 'appears stationary': the same-speed same-direction case gives zero relative speed, which is why one object looks frozen beside the other — this is a frame effect, not the object being truly at rest in all frames.

Do not teach that one observer's description is the 'real' motion and another's is 'just an optical illusion': all frame-relative descriptions are equally valid, and ambiguity is resolved by naming a frame.

Treat the boat-crossing-river example qualitatively at this age: it is a vivid frame-switch illustration, but its full relative velocity involves perpendicular (vector) addition that goes beyond the add/subtract speed rule targeted here.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Two of the three sources are marked verified:false in the row (the Alstein et al. 2021 review and Scherr et al. 2001); treat their claims as cited but not independently re-checked here.

Self-audit of arithmetic: oncoming cars at 50 and 40 close at 90 (50+40); same direction they close/separate at 10 (50−40); same-speed same-direction gives relative speed 0. These were checked and are consistent with the add/subtract rule.

The 'add when moving towards/away' phrasing is the original row's shorthand for opposite-direction motion; same-direction motion (including moving apart) subtracts. Feedback and summary tie each number to a named frame to keep this unambiguous.

The 'real vs apparent / optical illusion' misconception appears in the row's commonMisconceptions but in no sources[].claim, so it is confronted in Activity 4 feedback and the constraints without being attributed to a cited source.

The Scherr et al. claim was removed from the two-train departure activity because it concerns simultaneity and shared frames, not that activity's discrimination principle; it is retained only in the consolidation activity, which does address observers at rest sharing a frame.

The original 3D-interactive note ('3D adds cost without proportional gain') and conversation note ('dialogue cannot show' the recompute) are catalog-fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws; they are softened: a spatial 3D frame-switch may genuinely help cases like spacecraft docking or overtaking where depth matters, and a Socratic interview ('tell me what you think the other driver sees') can usefully elicit and name intuitions as a reflective companion. These alternatives are preserved as options with stated affordances/limits rather than dismissed.

The original recommendation's claim that live state is 'the essence' and that only a frame toggle can make the idea 'click' has been scoped as a strong proposal with a stated affordance (switchable state makes the comparison explicit) rather than an assertion of unique necessity over other media.

The boat-crossing-river and passing-car scenarios from the original were restored into Activity 1 as alternative frame-switch examples so they are genuinely present, not merely listed; the boat case is kept qualitative because its quantitative treatment needs vector addition beyond this age band.

assess.poeTask: Walk two students side by side at the same steady pace across the room. Ask the class to predict how fast each walker sees the OTHER moving, and WHY, before asking the walkers. Predicting 'the same speed as we see them' (an absolute answer) versus 'the other one looks stationary' surfaces the frame idea — the same-speed pair appearing still to each other is the key observation.
probeDeeper: Two cars drive side by side at the same 60 mph. How fast does each appear to move as seen from the other, and why does it look stationary?
You're on the train — is the platform moving? Answer from the train's frame AND the platform's frame.
Two cars approach each other, one at 50 and one at 40. How fast do they close on each other? What if they were going the same way?
Is there any experiment inside a smoothly moving train that could tell you you're moving, without looking outside?
assess.correctAnswer: Motion is defined relative to a chosen frame of reference. Looking only at the other train, all you can see is that the gap is changing — your train going forwards and their train going backwards look identical. Which is 'really' moving depends on the frame: relative to the platform/ground, whichever train's position changes is the one moving; but relative to the other train, each sees the other move. There is no single 'really moving' without saying relative to what.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'One of the trains is REALLY moving and the other really isn't — there's a true answer without saying compared to what.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make the student state the frame every time ('moving relative to what?'); switch frames on the same scene so each train is 'the mover' in turn.
errorPatterns.distractor: One train is really moving and the other really isn't — there's a single true answer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Won't accept the view is ambiguous and picks a 'true' mover.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Whatever the background scenery is doing tells you who's moving — the mover is the one the trees go past.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish the chosen frame from the scenery; on a featureless view (two trains, no ground) the motion is symmetric.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Equates the reference frame with the visible background rather than a chosen observer.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'To get the relative speed you always ADD the two speeds together.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Same direction -> subtract, opposite -> add; check with the same-speed same-direction case (relative speed zero -> appears stationary).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Adds speeds for two objects moving the SAME direction (should subtract).

responseLevels.gap: Insists one object is 'really' moving with no frame stated, or reads motion off the background scenery; adds or subtracts speeds by habit.
responseLevels.full: Explains motion as defined only relative to a chosen frame, resolves the ambiguous two-train view by naming the frame, and computes relative speed correctly for same-direction (subtract) and opposite (add) cases — including the same-speed-same-direction 'appears stationary' result.
responseLevels.partial: Says 'it depends on your point of view' and can compute a relative speed in one case, but doesn't consistently name the frame, or muddles same-direction versus opposite-direction relative speed — states the idea without applying it both ways.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Two trains sit side by side at a platform. Yours begins to move smoothly and, looking only out of the window at the other train, it seems as though the OTHER train is sliding backwards. For a moment you can't tell which train is really moving. How can the same view mean either 'we are moving' or 'they are moving' — and what decides which is true?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Students treat motion as an absolute property and give the ground/Earth a privileged frame. A student who grasps relative motion says the view is genuinely ambiguous and resolves it only by naming a reference frame (ground versus the other train). A student with the misconception insists one train is 'really' moving regardless of frame, or reads the motion off the background scenery as if the scenery IS the motion.
